body: Hong Kong is in southern China, borders Guangdong province, and is a Special Administrative Region, counted as part of China.
Hong Kong vehicles have white front plates and yellow rear plates, with some showing extra black mainland China plates.
Hong Kong drives on the left, similar to Singapore, but unlike Taiwan which drives on the right.
Hong Kong's dense urban areas feature modern skyscrapers and busy vibrant streets with a unique city vibe.
Rural Hong Kong is mountainous with green subtropical vegetation, low-rise buildings, and widespread non-urban road coverage.
Tall apartment buildings are a hallmark of Hong Kong architecture, much taller than those in Singapore or Taiwan.
Air conditioners mounted on building walls are very common due to Hong Kong's subtropical climate.
Hong Kong has two official languages: English and Chinese (mostly Cantonese). Bilingual signage is widespread.
Common grey lamp posts with wide bases and white stickers are seen throughout Hong Kong.
In rural Hong Kong, cylindrical wooden utility poles can be found, often with counters or transformers.
Striped kerbs are almost never seen; grey pedestrian guardrails are common instead.
Yellow pedestrian crossings and intersection grids are a feature of Hong Kong streets.
Hong Kong roads have white center lines and white or yellow outer lines, with concrete roads common.
Road signs are white rectangles with a black border and bilingual text.
Give way signs feature upside-down white triangles, thick red borders, and bilingual text.
Distinct weathered rock walls and green or blue plaques are common on mountain sides.
Red fire hydrants with circular tops and three protrusions are standard, alongside a pipe-like variant.
Yellow bollards with a white arrow in a blue circle are common at crossings and elsewhere.
Bright orange bins are a distinctive sight on Hong Kong sidewalks.
Hong Kong taxis are usually sedans with silver roofs and green bumper stickers; color varies by region, with red, green, or blue taxis.
Double-decker buses are standard and come in various color schemes. Minibuses with red or green roofs are also common.
Boxy multi-storey houses are common in villages, especially north of Hong Kong.
A double-decker tram line runs along northern Hong Kong Island; do not confuse this with the MTR railway.
Mong Kok and nearby Kowloon districts are known for crowded gridded streets and older apartments above shops, lacking glass walls.
North-west Hong Kong near the border is flat, with rice paddies and visible Shenzhen skyline to the north.
Central District is defined by modern skyscrapers, a bustling, affluent feel, and many luxury brand stores.
The IFC (rounder) is on Hong Kong Island, and the ICC (cuboid, straighter edges) is in Kowloon; these landmarks help orient location.
Mid-Levels district is known for non-identical tall modern apartments and hilly terrain.
Sai Wan Ho features many identical white and brown apartment blocks and tall glass office buildings.
Chek Lap Kok Island and the Boundary Crossing Facilities have major construction works and connecting bridges.
Caribbean Coast and Tung Chung have identical apartment blocks and rows of palm trees between and beside roads.
The Tsing Ma Bridge features two ladder-like towers with yellow and red guardrails and is one of three suspension bridges.
Ting Kau Bridge connects Ting Kau and Tsing Yi with three cylindrical towers and yellow paint in the median and sides.
Unlike the others, Stonecutters Bridge is identified by its lack of yellow paint and box beam guardrails.
Lung Wo Road provides views of the Hong Kong Island skyline south and Kowloon skyline north, and has clean sidewalks.
Tai Chung Kiu Road runs NE with Shing Mun River views, palm trees in the median, and a bike path beside it.
Fan Kam Road runs NE through dense tropical vegetation and small villages, sometimes with mountain views.
Lam Kam Road runs EW, with heavier traffic, more roadside houses, and a tree-lined median near villages.
Kai Tak Cruise Terminal is recognized by its shiny cylindrical shape and triangular windows.
The Hong Kong-Zhuhai-Macao Bridge stretches across the ocean, identified by black and yellow barriers.
Roads to Disneyland have palm trees and distinctive teal street lamps.
Peng Chau, Cheung Chau, and Lamma Island have narrow streets, rural architecture, and lack cars. Lamma is the hilliest.
Lugard Road around Victoria Peak features a black guardrail, skyline views, and tourists.
